components.text: Whether the resurrection inference actually identifies the specifically Christian God rather than supporting only generic supernatural agency.
Whether the Kalam-derived cause supplies specifically Christian rather than religion-neutral identification.
Whether the freedom explanation distinguishes Christianity from other religious explanations.
Generic causal reasoning does not identify the specifically Christian God.
The freedom argument is likewise available to multiple theistic religions.
Whether the resurrection supplies the missing Christian identification is deferred rather than assessed here.
Whether any part of the cumulative case identifies the inferred deity specifically with Christianity.
The resurrection argument is offered as the specifically Christian identifying component.
Whether the Christian God’s goals predict more unmistakable public evidence than is observed.
Whether sincere nonbelief and unmet seeking remain compatible with God’s aim of freely formed trust.
The expected disclosure is moderated by God's alleged aim of freely formed trust and loyalty.
The reply asserts adequate general evidence but does not directly explain sincere unanswered seeking or competing revelations.
Whether the felt ability to do otherwise verifies actual libertarian alternative possibilities.
Whether libertarian freedom coheres with an omniscient creator selecting a complete world history.
The felt impression of alternative possibility does not verify actual ability to do otherwise.
Classical divine foreknowledge and world selection allegedly conflict with libertarian choice.
Whether the Kalam syllogism derives a transcendent personal agent rather than only some cause of the universe.
The syllogism's stated conclusion is only that the universe has a cause, not that the cause is an agent or God.
Whether the proposed minimal historical facts are confirmable enough to support a resurrection comparison.
Whether scholarly assessment and reported sincerity can substitute for the underlying historical data.
The alleged minimal facts require confirmable underlying data before explanatory comparison.
Scholarly assessment and sincerity do not substitute for the historical evidence itself.
What level and type of evidence should be required for a worldview-altering resurrection claim.
Whether evidential demands may properly rise with the extraordinary scope of a divine-cause conclusion.
A worldview-altering resurrection claim requires stronger evidence than an ordinary familiar claim.
Whether the absence of a single science-like detector prevents reliable inquiry into God or historical events.
Whether philosophy and history can supply claim-appropriate evidence outside direct instrumental detection.
Different domains may require philosophical and historical methods rather than a single science-like detector.
The reply supports methodological plurality but does not deny that stronger claims need stronger evidence.
Whether philosophy actually supplies a warranted method for knowing the universe cause’s assigned attributes.
Whether a cause of the universe is adequately identified as an agent or God.
Granting a cause leaves both its identity and the method for knowing its attributes undetermined.
Naming philosophy as a method does not supply the missing attribute warrants.
How a timeless cause of the first temporal event can be identified as an agent rather than an impersonal state.
What independent post-Kalam argument supports adding agency to the bare causal conclusion.
Agent causation is proposed to explain transition from a timeless state to the first temporal event.
The response supplies a supplementary argument beyond the bare Kalam syllogism.
Whether divine knowledge of a future choice causally determines that choice and thereby removes freedom.
Whether divine selection of a complete foreknown world leaves genuine alternative possibilities available.
Divine knowledge of a future choice is distinguished from causally determining that choice.
The stronger world-selection and modal-settledness objection is not fully answered.
Whether Christian theism admits conditions that could count against or falsify it.
What strength of contrary historical evidence could rationally overturn Christian theism.
Christian theism is said to face potential defeat from contradiction or strong contrary historical evidence.
A rival supernatural-seeming event is not accepted as automatically identifying its source or falsifying Christianity.
Whether people can freely choose the intellectual belief that is treated as a precondition for trusting God.
Whether all relevant human mental states and decisions exemplify libertarian voluntary choice.
Whether distinguishing causal determination from knowledge establishes voluntariness of belief.
Belief formation is denied to be a voluntary exercise of libertarian choice.
The distinction bears on whether withholding clearer evidence preserves freely chosen belief or trust.
The move does not address whether foreknowledge causes or modally fixes choices.
Whether the large raw count of New Testament variants establishes pervasive textual uncertainty or corrupt revelation.
Whether openly identified disputed passages count as the kind of unclear disclosure predicted to be absent.
Whether manuscript abundance and disclosed variants establish the truth or divine source of Christian claims.
Raw variant totals are contextualized by their distribution across thousands of manuscripts.
Openly identified disputed passages are argued not to establish pervasive textual corruption.
